'''William Martin Boyce''' (born April 21, 1938) is an American [[mathematician]], [[credit analyst]], and [[computer scientist]].

== Education and career ==
Boyce received [[Bachelor of Arts|B.A.]] and [[Master of Science|M.S.]] degrees in [[mathematics]] from [[Florida State University]] in 1959 and 1960, respectively. From 1963 to 1965, Boyce served as an officer in the [[U.S. Army]] on the staff of the [[U.S. Army Security Agency]] Training Center and School. In 1965, he joined [[Project Apollo]] at [[NASA]] and was head of the Navigational Analysis Section from 1966 to 1967. He received a [[Ph.D.]] in mathematics from [[Tulane University]] in 1967.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Boyce |first1=W. |last2=Garey |first2=M. |date= 1973|title=Computing an Average Cost Allocation for Interrelated Operations |journal=IEEE Transactions on Manufacturing Technology |language=en |volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=15–22 |doi=10.1109/TMFT.1973.1135504 |issn=0046-838X}}</ref>

Boyce's 1967 [[doctoral thesis]] addressed the [[common fixed point problem]], resolving an [[unsolved mathematical problem]] first posed 13 years earlier by demonstrating the existence of commuting functions without a common [[Fixed point (mathematics)|fixed point]] and proving the conjecture to be false.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Boyce |first=William M. |date=1969 |title=Commuting Functions with No Common Fixed Point |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1994788 |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |volume=137 |pages=77–92 |doi=10.2307/1994788 |jstor=1994788 |issn=0002-9947}}</ref> His research involved the concept of [[Baxter permutation|Baxter permutations]], a term he coined to describe a class of [[permutations]] related to the fixed points of commuting functions, based on criteria defined by [[Glen E. Baxter|Glen Baxter]] in 1963. Boyce developed a [[Fortran|FORTRAN]] program to generate Baxter permutations and search for counterexamples to the common fixed point problem,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Boyce |first=William M. |date=1967 |title=Generation of a Class of Permutations Associated with Commuting Functions |url=https://oeis.org/A001181/a001181_1.pdf |journal=Mathematical Algorithms |volume=2 |pages=19–26}}</ref> making this thesis one of the earliest examples of a [[computer-assisted proof]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Brown |first1=Robert F. |date=January 2014 |title=A Good Question Won't Go Away: An Example Of Mathematical Research |url= |journal=American Mathematical Monthly |access-date= |quote=Since computers only became generally available to researchers in the 1950s, this 1967 example must have been one of the first uses of a computer to solve an abstract mathematical problem.}}</ref> His 1981 paper, "Baxter Permutations and Functional Composition,"<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Boyce |first=W. M. |date=1981 |title=Baxter Permutations and Functional Composition |url=https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?repid=rep1&type=pdf&doi=20d5adaa3c193418c3ca6a6825aef925c0a35294 |journal=Houston Journal of Economics |volume=7 |issue=2}}</ref> explored Baxter permutations beyond the context of commuting functions.<ref name="mcdowell">{{Cite journal |last=McDowell |first=Eric L. |date=5 August 2009 |title=Coincidence Values of Commuting Functions |url=https://topology.nipissingu.ca/tp/reprints/v34/tp34025.pdf |journal=Topology Proceedings |volume=34 |pages=365–384}}</ref>

After receiving his Ph.D., Boyce joined [[Bell Labs|Bell Laboratories]] in 1967. In 1970, he became head of the Mathematics Analysis Department.<ref>{{Cite news |date=July 2, 1970 |title=Moving to the Top |work=Echoes-Sentinel |pages=9}}</ref> During his time there, he created an improved [[computer algorithm]] for calculating [[Euclidean minimum spanning tree|minimal Euclidean]] [[Steiner tree problem|Steiner trees]], which he published as "STEINER 72" and "STEINER 73".<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Boyce |first1=W. M. |last2=Seery |first2=J. B. |title=STEINER 72, an improved version of Cockayne and Schiller's program STEINER for the minimal network problem |journal=Bell Laboratories Comp. Sci. Technical Report |volume=35}}</ref>

In the early 1970s, Boyce began to work on stochastic [[Bond (finance)|bond]] [[pricing model]]s for the [[Bell System]] and, in collaboration with [[Andrew Kalotay]], created strategies for optimizing the [[refunding]] of [[callable bond]]s. In contrast with then-existing strategies, which recommended that an issue be called when rates reached a certain level below the issue's coupon, Boyce and Kalotay showed that it sometimes makes sense to wait, and introduced the notion of refunding efficiency to quantify the value lost when an issue is called too early.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kalotay |first1=Andrew J. |last2=Yang |first2=Deane |last3=Fabozzi |first3=Frank J. |date=May 2007 |title=Refunding efficiency: a generalized approach |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/17446540600771076 |journal=Applied Financial Economics Letters |language=en |volume=3 |issue=3 |pages=141–146 |doi=10.1080/17446540600771076 |issn=1744-6546|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Bell System companies applied these strategies and were able to save millions of dollars in financing costs. Boyce and Kalotay described their refunding strategy in their 1979 papers, "Optimum Bond Calling and Refunding"<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Boyce |first1=W. M. |last2=Kalotay |first2=A. J. |date=1979 |title=Optimum Bond Calling and Refunding |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/25059810 |journal=Interfaces |volume=9 |issue=5 |pages=36–49 |doi=10.1287/inte.9.5.36 |jstor=25059810 |issn=0092-2102}}</ref> (which was a runner-up for the 1979 Management Science Achievement Award<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Barry |first=John Y. |date=1979 |title=The Management Science Achievement Award |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/25059807 |journal=Interfaces |volume=9 |issue=5 |pages=1–2 |doi=10.1287/inte.9.5.1 |jstor=25059807 |issn=0092-2102}}</ref>) and "Tax Differentials and Callable Bonds."<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Boyce |first1=W. M. |last2=Kalotay |first2=A. J. |date=1979 |title=Tax Differentials and Callable Bonds |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2327050 |journal=The Journal of Finance |volume=34 |issue=4 |pages=825–838 |doi=10.2307/2327050 |jstor=2327050 |issn=0022-1082}}</ref>

Following the [[Breakup of the Bell System|Bell System breakup]], Kalotay invited Boyce to join him at the investment bank [[Salomon Brothers]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kalotay |first=Andrew |title=Let's Assume Taxes |url=https://www.stories.finance/stories/kalotay}}</ref>
